titleText.es: Debería mejorar pronto... Ahora que la Apple Store abandona el DRM, Cory Doctorow dejará el muñeco vudú de Steve Jobs.
titleText.en: He should be better soon -- now that the Apple Store is getting rid of DRM, Cory Doctorow will get rid of his Steve Jobs voodoo doll.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive preserves the title-text joke about Apple dropping DRM and Cory Doctorow giving up a Steve Jobs voodoo doll; the English text is the exact official image title.

regions.labelEs: ¿EH? STEVE JOBS NO DA NINGUNA PONENCIA ESTE AÑO, ALEGANDO UNA ENORME PÉRDIDA DE PESO DEBIDO A UN PROBLEMA HORMONAL.

excludedUnits.rationale: Steve Jobs is an unchanged personal name rather than Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: No stays before da even though ninguna supplies another negative word after the verb.
Da is the matching form of dar, ninguna replaces una under the negative frame, and ponencia names the formal talk.
Alegando adds the simultaneous act of citing an explanation for the preceding decision.
Enorme has one singular form for both genders, so it already matches the feminine singular noun pérdida.
Pérdida names the loss, de connects it to what changes, and peso identifies weight.
Debido a introduces un problema hormonal as the stated cause.
Un is masculine because problema is masculine despite its final -a.
Problema names the condition first, and the neutral descriptive adjective hormonal follows it.
Hormonal has one singular form for both genders, so it already agrees with the masculine singular noun problema.

regions.labelEs: UNA PENA. SEGURO QUE APPLE ESTABA DESEANDO PRESENTAR AL CEO MÁS DELGADO Y LIGERO DEL MUNDO.

excludedUnits.rationale: Apple is an unchanged company name rather than Spanish vocabulary.
CEO is an unchanged English business initialism rather than Spanish lexical text.

applications.explanationEn: Seguro que opens the speaker's strongly expected claim.
Estaba places the eagerness in an ongoing past state, deseando supplies the strong desire, and presentar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Estaba uses the imperfect because the eagerness is presented as an ongoing past state.
Al combines the personal a with el before the specific person identified by the adjacent title.

applications.exampleEs: AL CEO MÁS DELGADO Y LIGERO
applications.explanationEn: Al contains the matching article el, más marks the highest degree, and delgado y ligero supplies two coordinated descriptions of the same person.
Delgado and ligero use masculine singular -o because both describe one male person.
Del introduces mundo as the larger group within which the comparison is made.

cards.noteEn: Eh can show that the speaker is surprised or did not understand what was just said.

example.en: Huh? I didn't hear you.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.noteEn: Da is a present form of dar for one person or thing, or for formal singular you. With ponencia, dar means to give or deliver a formal talk.

example.es: La profesora da una ponencia mañana.
example.en: The professor is giving a talk tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone gives or delivers a formal talk?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of dar with una ponencia; replace una with another small specifying word when needed.
cards.noteEn: Dar changes for the person and time: doy, da, damos, dio, and so on. Ponencia stays the name of the formal talk. A word such as una, alguna, or ninguna can come before it.

example.es: Marta dio una ponencia sobre salud.
example.en: Marta gave a talk about health.

cards.noteEn: A ponencia is a formal presentation, often at a conference or professional event.

example.es: La ponencia empieza a las diez.
example.en: The talk starts at ten.

cards.questionEn: What marketing language turns the description of the CEO into a joke?
cards.answerEn: Apple product presentations often emphasize devices as exceptionally thin and light; the speaker applies that product language to a person.
cards.noteEn: Steve Jobs was Apple's CEO and delivered its prominent keynote presentations. The comic turns his reported weight loss into a grim parody of a product unveiling.
Alegando is the -ando form of alegar. It can add the reason or explanation that someone gives for another action.

example.en: She canceled the meeting, citing tiredness.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

example.en: She came in running.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to a loss of body weight?
cards.answerEn: Use pérdida de peso for ‘weight loss.’
cards.noteEn: Pérdida names a loss, de connects it to what is lost, and peso names weight. The three words form a conventional health-related combination.

example.es: La pérdida de peso fue gradual.
example.en: The weight loss was gradual.

cards.answerEn: due; because of (as part of debido a)
cards.noteEn: Debido joins a to form the connector debido a, which introduces a cause.

example.es: El partido se canceló debido a la lluvia.
example.en: The game was canceled because of the rain.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce the cause of something with the meaning ‘due to’ or ‘because of’?
cards.answerEn: Use debido a, then name the cause.
cards.noteEn: Debido remains masculine singular in this connector, and a stays directly after it. The cause can be a noun or a longer naming phrase. Debido a is common in neutral and formal explanations.

example.es: El vuelo se retrasó debido a la niebla.
example.en: The flight was delayed because of the fog.

cards.answerEn: to; completes debido a (‘due to; because of’)
cards.noteEn: This a stays after debido and introduces the cause that follows.

example.es: Llegamos tarde debido a un accidente.
example.en: We arrived late because of an accident.

cards.promptEs: el/un problema y otros sustantivos masculinos en -ma
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish say un problema even though problema ends in -a?
cards.answerEn: Problema is masculine, so use el or un and masculine describing words with it.
cards.noteEn: A noun's ending is only a clue to its gender, not an absolute rule. Several common words of Greek origin ending in -ma are masculine, including el problema, el sistema, el tema, and el programa. Learn each noun together with its article because not every word ending in -ma follows this pattern.

example.en: The problem is small.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.noteEn: Pena can name sorrow or distress. In una pena, it commonly expresses that something is unfortunate or disappointing.

example.es: Fue una pena perder el tren.
example.en: It was a shame to miss the train.

cards.noteEn: Seguro que is a common conversational opener for something the speaker strongly expects to be true. Seguro stays masculine singular in this use.

example.en: I'm sure Marta will arrive soon.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce something you strongly expect to be true?
cards.answerEn: Put seguro que before the statement: it means ‘I'm sure…’ or ‘I bet…’.
cards.noteEn: Treat seguro que as a conversational opener here. Seguro stays masculine singular, and que introduces the statement the speaker expects to be true.

example.es: Seguro que Ana ya lo sabe.
example.en: I'm sure Ana already knows.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: it was; used to be (a past state)

cards.promptEs: estar deseando + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is eager or looking forward to doing something?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of estar, then deseando, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only estar changes for the person and time: estoy, está, estaba, and so on. Deseando stays unchanged, and the final action keeps its dictionary ending in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.en: We are looking forward to traveling.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: After a form of estar, deseando can show strong eagerness for the action that follows.

example.en: We are eager to travel.

cards.noteEn: Presentar can introduce a person to an audience or unveil something publicly.

example.es: Van a presentar el nuevo diseño.
example.en: They are going to unveil the new design.

cards.answerEn: a + el before a specific person; often “the” or “to the” in English
cards.noteEn: Spanish contracts a + el to al. The personal a can mark a specific person who receives or is affected by an action; English may use “the,” “to the,” or no separate preposition, depending on the verb.

example.en: I see the teacher.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

example.en: I know Marta.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe someone or something as the most of a quality?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of “the,” name the person or thing, then add más plus the describing word.
cards.noteEn: The opening el, la, los, or las agrees with the noun. Más stays unchanged, while the final adjective changes when Spanish normally requires agreement.

example.en: It is the longest street.

cards.noteEn: Más normally means “more.” After el, la, los, or las, it can instead mark the highest degree in a group: la más rápida means “the fastest one.”

example.en: Ana is the fastest.

cards.noteEn: Ligero can describe something that has little weight. In other contexts it can also mean quick or slight.

example.en: I'm looking for a lightweight laptop.

cards.answerEn: in the; introduces the group used for a ‘most’ or ‘least’ comparison
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After a description with más or menos that picks out an extreme, it can introduce the larger group being compared. Natural English often uses ‘in the’ rather than translating de literally as ‘of.’

example.es: Es el edificio más alto del barrio.
example.en: It is the tallest building in the neighborhood.
